AdvisorError.description:
The 503 ``AI_NOT_CONFIGURED`` / 429 ``RATE_LIMITED`` envelope.

Mirrors ``ReceiptError``/``StatsError``: one ``detail`` string code across the
API. NOT the shape of a mid-stream failure — that is an SSE ``error`` frame
inside a 200 (see the route's response description).
AdvisorError.title: AdvisorError

AdvisorTurn.description: One replayed turn. ``role`` is the Anthropic role, not a user role.
AdvisorTurn.title: AdvisorTurn

DecisionCounts.description: "What will happen on apply" (§10.4) — the numbers the confirmation shows.
DecisionCounts.title: DecisionCounts

FxConvertRead.description:
GET /fx/convert response (D8): the conversion plus the echoed request.

``converted_minor``/``rate``/``rate_as_of`` are null TOGETHER when no rate can
be resolved for the pair — the client shows "no rate available" and offers the
manual-override field. ``rate`` is a decimal STRING (never a float) quantized
to 8 dp for display; the math behind ``converted_minor`` uses the full-precision
rate. ``rate_as_of`` is the stored row's own date, which may be older than the
requested date (nearest-previous resolution, disclosed honestly).
FxConvertRead.title: FxConvertRead

GoalItemFileCreated.description: POST response: the row (always unconfirmed) + where to PUT the bytes.
GoalItemFileCreated.title: GoalItemFileCreated

GoalItemFileRead.description: One attachment as the list and the confirm route return it.
GoalItemFileRead.title: GoalItemFileRead

GoalItemRead.description:
One node, with every number the server computed for it.

The client assembles the TREE from ``parent_id``; it computes no money, no
depth and no inherited date — those are answers, not raw data.
GoalItemRead.title: GoalItemRead

GoalRead.description:
List-item AND single-GET shape (D12) — computed fields included.

The single GET runs the same whole-portfolio assembler as the list, so
``allocated_monthly_minor`` is identical in both (AM-4 consistency).
GoalRead.title: GoalRead

LimitRead.description: PUT response — a write carries no period context, hence no ``spent``.
LimitRead.title: LimitRead

PeriodBounds.description:
Resolved window, echoed. ``from`` is a Python keyword — hence the alias
(the ``FxConvertRead.from_currency`` precedent).
PeriodBounds.title: PeriodBounds

PeriodTotals.description:
The ``previous`` block: totals only.

No ``by_category`` (D4): the comparison screen compares totals, and a
per-category diff view is additive later if it is ever asked for.
PeriodTotals.title: PeriodTotals

PeriodUnit.description: The four period grammars (D5). Wire values; used as a query enum.
PeriodUnit.title: PeriodUnit

PresignedUpload.description:
The presigned PUT the client uploads its JPEG to.

``headers`` is **advisory**: it carries ``{"Content-Type": "image/jpeg"}`` as a
hint the client SHOULD send, but storage does not enforce it (minio-py signs the
host only, never the content-type — see services/storage.py / senior-lead V1).
The real size gate is the parse-time HEAD ``Content-Length`` check (S3).
PresignedUpload.title: PresignedUpload

RateLimitedError.description: 429 body — one error envelope across the API (AM-I).
RateLimitedError.title: RateLimitedError

ReceiptCreated.description: POST /receipts response: the new row's id + status + where to upload.
ReceiptCreated.title: ReceiptCreated

StatementApplyReport.description:
What an apply DID — the response body and nowhere else (§10.6).

Not persisted (v1): the durable record is the session's ``applied`` status plus
the transactions themselves, and a stored report would be a second truth that
can disagree with them.

The four numbers add up to the session's row count: ``skipped`` is exactly the
``decision=skip`` cross-section the confirmation screen showed, and every other
row ended in one of the three others. They are NOT a partition by row, and
deliberately so: several ``similar`` rows may point at one record of the user's,
which is deleted once. ``replaced`` therefore counts the records that
disappeared, ``created`` the rest of what was written, and their sum is exactly
the number of transactions this call inserted.
StatementApplyReport.title: StatementApplyReport

StatementBulkDecision.description:
One decision for every row of one match status (§10.8).

Deliberately keyed by ``match_status`` and not by a list of row ids: the whole
point is "keep all my own records" / "import everything new" on a thousand-row
statement, and a client that had to enumerate ids would first have to page
through them all.
StatementBulkDecision.title: StatementBulkDecision

StatementFormatsRead.description:
What the upload accepts: the ``PARSERS`` keys, in registry order.

Plain strings, deliberately not an enum: a new bank is a line in the registry,
and the point of this route is that the client learns about it WITHOUT being
rebuilt. The web keeps the human names; an id it has no name for is rendered
as the id itself rather than hidden.
StatementFormatsRead.title: StatementFormatsRead

StatementImportError.description:
404/422 envelope — the ``DepositError`` shape with the refusal's facts (§10.7).

``detail`` is the stable UPPER_SNAKE code, as everywhere in this API. The
optional fields are populated for exactly two refusals, each of which is
unusable without them — one error model rather than several, so the routes'
``anyOf`` union stays a single reference:

* ``STATEMENT_CURRENCY_MISMATCH`` — "this file is in BYN, that account is in
  USD" is the whole content of the refusal, and a client that had to re-derive
  it from two other requests would show the user a dead end;
* ``REPLACE_CONFIRMATION_MISMATCH`` (S3) — the number the user confirmed and
  the number the server would really delete RIGHT NOW. The second is what the
  replace preview would answer on a re-read, so the client can redraw the
  warning instead of asking the user to guess what changed.
StatementImportError.title: StatementImportError

StatementReplacePreview.description:
What ``POST /replace`` would destroy — counted BEFORE anything is confirmed.

The whole point of the replace path is that it deletes transactions the
statement will not necessarily bring back in the same shape (a receipt link, a
plan payment, an attribution to a recurring template all die with the row), so
the warning has to be built from the SERVER's own selection rather than from
anything a client counted for itself.

Reading it mutates nothing and is repeatable: the numbers may legitimately move
between two reads if the user books something meanwhile, which is exactly why
``POST /replace`` re-checks them against ``confirm_deleted_total`` instead of
trusting the number this response carried.

``deleted_total + transfers_kept`` is EVERY row the account shows in
``[from; period_to]`` — a non-transfer row can only ever be seen through its
own ``account_id``, and a transfer through either leg. So the two numbers
together say what happens to everything the user can see in that range, and
nothing survives unannounced.
StatementReplacePreview.title: StatementReplacePreview

StatementReplaceReport.description:
What a replace DID — the response body and nowhere else (§10.6).

Deliberately NOT ``StatementApplyReport``: that report's ``skipped`` and
``replaced`` describe per-row decisions, and a replace has none — it wipes a
date range and re-files the statement over it. Reusing those names would let a
reader believe a replace honoured decisions it explicitly ignores.
StatementReplaceReport.title: StatementReplaceReport

StatementReplaceRequest.description:
The confirmed replace (architecture §7 + the S3 delta).

``confirm_deleted_total`` is the number the user read off the preview and typed
back. It is TWO guards in one: a click cannot land on a destructive button by
accident, and the server re-checks the number against what it is really about
to delete — so data booked between the preview and the confirmation cannot be
swept away by a number that was true a minute ago.
StatementReplaceRequest.title: StatementReplaceRequest

StatementRowCandidate.description:
A transaction the matcher pointed at, in mini form (§10.5).

Embedded in the row rather than referenced by id: a preview screen with a
thousand rows must not fire a thousand lookups to answer "which of my records
is this?". JOINed at read time from ``candidate_tx_ids``, so a transaction
deleted meanwhile simply stops being reported instead of becoming a dead id.
StatementRowCandidate.title: StatementRowCandidate

StatementRowList.description: The pagination envelope of ``GET /{id}/rows`` (the TransactionList shape).
StatementRowList.title: StatementRowList

StatementRowPatch.description:
The user's decision on ONE row (§10.3).

Both fields are optional and independent — the preview edits them from two
different controls, and a category click must not resend (or silently reset) a
decision the user made a minute ago.

``category_id`` is TRI-STATE by presence, the project's PATCH grammar: omitted
keeps what is there, a value sets it, an explicit ``null`` clears it back to
"no category". Sending a category — and nothing else in this API — is what
raises ``category_user_set``; an explicit ``null`` clears the choice and the
flag with it. That flag is the gate of the learning upsert, so the server's own
suggestion must never be able to teach the maps that made it.
StatementRowPatch.title: StatementRowPatch

TokenCreated.description: POST /tokens response — the ONLY place the plaintext ever appears.
TokenCreated.title: TokenCreated

TokenPair.description: Single shape for both /auth/login and /auth/refresh responses.
TokenPair.title: TokenPair

TokenSelf.description:
GET /tokens/self — what a token may learn about ITSELF, and nothing more.

No name, no timestamps, no list, no plaintext: the MCP client needs its scope
to decide which tools to publish, and it could have derived that from one
probe call anyway, so this leaks nothing (architecture §4).
TokenSelf.title: TokenSelf

UpcomingChargeRead.description:
One future occurrence of one template — a row of the /transactions widget.

Deliberately flat and self-contained: the widget merges occurrences ACROSS
templates in date order, so every field it renders comes stamped on the row and
the client never joins, converts or does date math of its own. ``currency`` is
the template's stamp (== its account's), so a multi-currency list renders each
row at its own exponent.
UpcomingChargeRead.title: UpcomingChargeRead

UpcomingDeadlineRead.description:
One row of ``GET /goals/upcoming`` — a plan node whose date is coming up.

The list crosses GOALS, so unlike :class:`GoalItemList` there is no single
currency to name once per response: every money field carries its own
currency ON THE ROW (AM-5). Rows of different currencies are never summed —
not by the client, and not by a model reading this through MCP.

There is no notification channel behind this: it feeds the in-app "coming up"
block, which is why the row carries what that block renders (whose plan, which
branch, how much, how much is already paid) and nothing else.
UpcomingDeadlineRead.title: UpcomingDeadlineRead

UserCreate.description: {email, password} (+ ignored privilege fields; safe=True drops them).
UserCreate.title: UserCreate

UserUpdate.description:
{email?, password?} only — privilege fields structurally absent (AM-A).

Extra fields are ignored (Pydantic default), not forbidden (AM-H/R4). The
``CreateUpdateDictModel`` base contributes no fields — only the
``create_update_dict`` helpers the stock users router invokes.
UserUpdate.title: UserUpdate

get.description:
The user's accounts, each with its computed balance (the categories shape).

``include_archived`` mirrors ``GET /categories`` exactly, and an archived
account still reports a real balance: the money on it did not stop existing
when the user stopped using it.

post.description: Create an account. No name-uniqueness check — categories has none either.

422.description: Business rule rejection (string code) or validation error

200.description:
Server-Sent Events stream of the answer. Frames:

- `event: delta` / `data: {"text": "..."}` — 0..n answer chunks; `data` is
  always ONE line of JSON, so a chunk may contain newlines and quotes.
- `event: done` / `data: {}` — terminal frame on success.
- `event: error` / `data: {"detail": "ANTHROPIC_ERROR"}` — terminal frame on
  failure, from any position INCLUDING before the first delta.

Exactly one terminal frame is emitted. The HTTP status is 200 in every case;
a failed answer is the `error` frame, never a 5xx.

REGISTER_USER_ALREADY_EXISTS.summary: A user with this email already exists.

detail.reason: Password should be at least 3 characters

get.description:
The user's deposits, archived ones INCLUDED (no ``include_archived`` param).

The one archive-inclusive cache entry the client dims itself: a closed deposit
still holds a balance and a history, and a list that hid it would hide money.

post.description: Create the deposit AND its hidden ledger account, in one transaction.

422.description: Business rule rejection (string code) or validation error
Business rule rejection (string code) or validation error

get.description:
Plan nodes across ALL live goals whose date lands in the next ``days`` (§6).

Declared BEFORE every ``/{goal_id}`` route in this module (see the module
docstring): after them, "upcoming" would be read as a goal id and 404.

A node is here for exactly one of two reasons, and the reminder wins: with a
reminder set, the REMINDER date decides alone — a node whose reminder has
already passed stays out even though its deadline is days away, because the
user chose when to be told. Without one, the effective (inherited) deadline
decides. Archived goals are absent entirely (§10d): archiving deletes nothing,
so unarchiving brings every row straight back.

No business 422 of its own — ``days`` is a bounded Query, so FastAPI's own
``HTTPValidationError`` is the only honest 422 arm (the ``/recurring/upcoming``
precedent) and no ``responses`` override is declared.

422.description: Business rule rejection (string code) or validation error
Business rule rejection (string code) or validation error
Business rule rejection (string code) or validation error

get.description: The goal's whole plan, flat, in ONE recursive statement (never N+1).

422.description: Business rule rejection (string code) or validation error

delete.description:
Delete the node AND its subtree; linked transactions survive, unlinked.

Both halves are constraints, not code (§3/§7): ``parent_id`` cascades over the
subtree, and ``transactions.goal_item_id`` is ON DELETE SET NULL — so no path
through this app, or through psql, can delete a user's money by deleting a
plan node. Attached FILES are removed with the rows by the same cascade, and
their stored objects are swept afterwards by a best-effort background job.

The object keys are collected BEFORE the delete, and that order is the whole
trick: once the CASCADE has run, nothing on this server knows what the subtree
used to hold. The sweep then runs after the COMMIT, so unreachable storage
cannot block a user from deleting their own node — the row is the truth, and
an orphaned object is a leak of disk, not of data (§7).

422.description: Business rule rejection (string code) or validation error
Business rule rejection (string code) or validation error

get.description:
The node's attachments, oldest first. Unpaginated — there are at most ten.

Readable on an ARCHIVED goal (no ``_reject_archived``): archiving hides a plan
from the active list, it does not take the user's own documents away.

schema.title: Response List Goal Item Files Goals  Goal Id  Items  Item Id  Files Get

post.description:
Reserve an attachment row and hand back the presigned PUT for its bytes.

The per-node cap is a plain COUNT with no lock — the same interface guard as
the per-goal item cap (§8): an eleventh attachment costs a crowded screen, not
money, and serializing uploads on a node-wide lock would be a real price for an
imaginary problem.

422.description: Business rule rejection (string code) or validation error

delete.description:
Delete the row, then the object — in that order, and never the reverse.

The DB is the truth (§7): the row goes first and is COMMITTED, so a failure
there is a failed request and is reported as one, never masked by a 204. Only
after that does the best-effort cleanup run in the background — unreachable
storage leaves an orphaned object (disk, not data: the key is only UUIDs) and
still answers 204, because the attachment genuinely is gone.

422.description: Business rule rejection (string code) or validation error

post.description:
Prove the object exists and is within size, then mark the row uploaded.

Taxonomy copied from the receipts parse gate, because it is the same probe:
unreachable/misbehaving storage → 503 ``STORAGE_UNAVAILABLE`` (a service
condition, never a 500 and never a client error), a missing object → 409
``FILE_NOT_UPLOADED`` with the row left UNCONFIRMED so the client can PUT and
retry, an oversized object → 422 ``IMAGE_TOO_LARGE`` against the SAME
``receipt_max_bytes`` ceiling as a receipt photo.

Confirming an already-confirmed file is a 200 no-op, and it short-circuits
BEFORE the probe: retries are ordinary here (a client that lost the response
will send it again), and re-probing could only ever demote a file the server
has already seen — a transient storage blip must not un-prove bytes.

422.description: Business rule rejection (string code) or validation error

get.description:
Monthly series for the chart, current month included, empty months as 0.

``saved_end_minor`` is cumulative and includes the pre-window base sum, so
the chart starts at the true balance (the client renders, never computes).

schema.title: Response Goal Progress Goals  Goal Id  Progress Get

get.description:
Every limit the user owns, each with its spend for ``month``.

``month`` defaults to the current UTC month (D16) — the screen that renders
this is "how am I doing right now", so requiring an anchor would make the
common call the verbose one. The response ECHOES the resolved month so a
client never has to reconstruct which window it is looking at.

delete.description:
Remove the limit. The category and its transactions are untouched.

The load is user_id-scoped, so a foreign limit and a missing one leave by the
same code path with a byte-identical body (no-oracle).

put.description:
Create or replace this category's limit. Idempotent by construction.

Guard order preserves the existence oracle: a foreign archived category is
CATEGORY_NOT_FOUND, never CATEGORY_ARCHIVED. System (shared, ``user_id IS
NULL``) categories are legal targets — they are what a fresh user has — and
the composite PK means each user's limit on a shared category is their own
row.

422.description: Business rule rejection (string code) or validation error

get.description:
The caller's settings; a user without a row reads as defaults, unwritten.

Deliberately NOT self-healing (the ``read_base_currency`` contract): a GET that
inserted a row would make a plain page load a write, and the defaults it would
persist are exactly the ones returned here anyway.

patch.description:
Set/clear the four settings; omitted fields are left untouched.

``model_fields_set`` owns the omitted-vs-explicit-null distinction, as
everywhere else in this codebase: omit keeps the stored value, an explicit null
clears it back to "not confirmed", a value overwrites. ``base_currency`` is the
one exception — a NOT NULL column, so its explicit null is a 422 rather than a
clear (the ``GoalUpdate`` precedent).

Both refusals fire BEFORE anything is committed, so a rejected PATCH leaves
the row (and a row this call self-healed into existence) exactly as it was.

422.description: Business rule rejection (string code) or validation error
Business rule rejection (string code) or validation error

get.description:
Every template the user owns — paused and ended ones included.

This list IS the management screen: a paused template is exactly what the
user came to resume, and an ended one is what they came to delete. Filtering
either out would hide the row from the only place it can be acted on.

422.description: Business rule rejection (string code) or validation error

get.description:
Every charge the live templates still owe in the next ``days`` days (B1-B5).

Declared BEFORE the parameterized routes below (the /transactions/summary
landmine): after them, "upcoming" would be parsed as a template id and 422.

The set is exactly "not yet materialized AND due today or later" — the shared
floor of ``upcoming_due_dates`` says so: a template already booked through
today carries ``watermark == today`` and drops today's row on its own, while a
template that is due today and has not run yet keeps it. A template in arrears
contributes only its FUTURE dates, never the pending past ones (the same rule
``next_due_on`` renders). Future-start templates ride in for free — their
watermark IS ``start - 1``.

Strictly READ-ONLY: this route never writes the watermark, so polling it can
neither book nor skip a charge. Paused templates are excluded (nothing is
owed); a template whose ACCOUNT was archived after the fact is NOT — the
materializer still books it (B2/MINOR-1), and hiding it would make the widget
lie about money that is going to move.

No business 422 of its own — ``days`` is a bounded Query, so the automatic
``HTTPValidationError`` is the only honest 422 arm (the ``stats_monthly``
precedent) and no ``responses`` override is declared.

422.description: Business rule rejection (string code) or validation error

post.description:
Parse a statement into a preview session for ``account_id``.

Gate ORDER (architecture §6): account → size → format → parse → currency → DB.
Everything that can refuse the request does so BEFORE a single row is written,
so a failed upload leaves nothing behind to clean up or to show.

422.description: Business rule rejection (string code) or validation error

get.description:
The formats the upload accepts, in registry order.

The registry is the single source of truth (services/statement_import/__init__),
so this route CANNOT drift from what ``POST`` validates against: adding a bank
is one line there and the control fills itself.

Authenticated like every other route here — the list is not a secret, but an
unauthenticated route in this router would be the one place where forgetting
the dependency has no other symptom. A PAT still gets 403 from the fail-closed
allowlist: import is out of MCP as a whole, and a route that only tells an
agent which parsers exist is of no use without the ones that follow it.

delete.description:
Cancel a preview. The rows go with it (``ON DELETE CASCADE``).

Only a ``parsed`` session can be cancelled: an applied or replaced one is a
JOURNAL of what was done to the user's money, and deleting it would erase the
record without undoing anything.

422.description: Business rule rejection (string code) or validation error

post.description:
Execute the session's decisions — the "reconcile" path (architecture §7).

ONE database transaction for the whole statement, in ``services/.../apply.py``:
a thousand rows must land together or not at all, and the session's status has
to move with them.

The report is the response body and nothing else (§10.6). ``skipped`` is taken
from ``_counts_of`` rather than counted again here, so the number the
confirmation dialog showed and the number the report shows are one query.

422.description: Business rule rejection (string code) or validation error

post.description:
The "replace from date X" path (architecture §7) — the scope's only deletion.

ONE database transaction in ``services/.../apply.py`` does all of it: the
delete, the re-filing of the statement over the emptied range and the session's
move to ``replaced``. A range half-wiped and half-refilled is the one outcome a
user could never repair by hand.

``confirm_deleted_total`` is checked against the DELETE's own ``RETURNING``, so
what is compared is the set that actually disappeared rather than a count taken
a moment earlier. A disagreement rolls everything back untouched and answers 422
with both numbers, and the client redraws the preview.

Per-row decisions are ignored here — see ``replace_import``.

422.description: Business rule rejection (string code) or validation error

get.description:
What ``POST /replace`` would destroy, counted BEFORE it is confirmed.

A read, and repeatable: it writes nothing, so a user may move the date around
until the numbers look right. The numbers are the SERVER's own selection — the
same predicate the delete runs — because a client that counted for itself would
be warning the user about a set nobody is going to delete.

Gate order: 404 (foreign == missing) → 422 IMPORT_FINISHED → 422
REPLACE_FROM_OUT_OF_RANGE. The lifecycle gate is a deliberate addition to the
architecture's table (plan §"Дельта S3", point 3): on an applied or replaced
session this would count the transactions THAT VERY SESSION just created as
"will be deleted", which is a misleading number printed over an operation
nobody can undo.

ONE grouped query answers all five transaction counters. Its base predicate is
"either leg of this account, in range", which splits exactly in two: a
non-transfer row can only be seen through its own ``account_id`` (the counter
trio is NULL on it, by CHECK), so the non-transfer half IS the delete's own
selection, and the transfer half is everything that survives. The two therefore
add up to every row the account shows in the range — nothing is left
unannounced, and the delete predicate and the warning cannot drift apart.

422.description: Business rule rejection (string code) or validation error

get.description: The preview, in FILE order, with each row's candidates embedded.

post.description:
One decision for every row of ONE match status (§10.8).

Keyed by the match status rather than by a list of ids: "keep all my own
records" is the actual gesture, and a client that had to enumerate ids would
first have to page through a thousand rows to name them.

It moves the DECISION and nothing else — the category a user picked on a row
survives a bulk "skip these", because those are two independent choices and the
second must not silently discard the first. Rows of the other statuses are
outside the WHERE clause and are not touched at all.

The answer is the session, whose counters come from the same ``_counts_of`` the
GET uses: what the confirmation screen shows after a bulk click has to be
exactly what apply will do, and a second counting implementation is exactly how
those two drift apart.

422.description: Business rule rejection (string code) or validation error

patch.description:
One row's decision and/or category. Answers with the UPDATED row (§10.3).

200 with the row rather than 204: the preview holds up to a thousand rows in a
paged infinite query, and a client that had to re-read them all to see the
effect of one click would page through the whole statement per click.

Gate order: session (404) → lifecycle (422) → row (404) → category (422) →
decision (422). The row lookup filters ``import_id`` AND ``row_id`` in ONE
query, so a row of somebody else's session — or of another session of one's
own — is indistinguishable from a row that does not exist, at BOTH levels.

422.description: Business rule rejection (string code) or validation error

get.description:
Trailing ``months`` calendar months, current (partial) month INCLUDED.

No business 422 of its own — ``months`` is a bounded Query, so the automatic
``HTTPValidationError`` is the only honest 422 arm and no ``responses``
override is declared.

422.description: Business rule rejection (string code) or validation error

get.description:
EXPENSE rows only — there is no ``kind`` knob.

"Куда уходят деньги" is the asked-for view; a "top income sources" screen was
never requested, and a knob nobody asked for is speculative config. Adding
``?kind=`` later is purely additive.

422.description: Business rule rejection (string code) or validation error

get.description: Every token the user owns, revoked ones included (the revocation is a fact).

post.description: Issue a token. The plaintext in the response is the ONLY copy that exists.

get.description: The calling token's own ``{id, scope}`` — no name, no timestamps, no list.

delete.description: Soft revoke. Foreign, missing and already-revoked share ONE 404 (no-oracle).

get.description:
The user's transactions, filtered and sorted, with the unpaged ``total``.

Every filter AND-composes (``_read_filters``, shared with ``GET /export``) and
``total`` counts the SAME filter set — the size of the result being paged
through, never the size of the table. ``q`` is a case-insensitive substring over
``merchant`` and ``note`` and nothing else; ``country`` is an exact match on the
row's ISO-3166-1 alpha-2 code.

The amount sorts compare RAW ``amount_minor`` and convert nothing: each row is
ordered by the number it actually carries, in its own currency. See ``_ORDER_BY``
for why that is the honest option rather than a shortcut.

post.description:
Create a transaction; a repeated ``client_id`` replays instead of duplicating.

FIRST WRITE WINS: the replay arm never consults the body, so a second POST with
the same key and a *different* payload returns the stored row untouched. Body
mismatch is deliberately not detected — the client mints the key once per
logical create and never mutates a queued item.

200.description: Idempotent replay — the existing transaction, not created

422.description: Business rule rejection (string code) or validation error

get.description:
Stream the user's transactions as CSV — the list's filters, no paging.

Filter parity with ``GET /transactions`` is mechanical, not copied — both call
``_read_filters``, so you export exactly what you are looking at. ``sort`` is the
one list parameter this route does NOT declare: FastAPI ignores query parameters a
route never declared, so sending it is a no-op rather than a 422, and the file
stays oldest-first (see the ORDER BY below for why that is a contract, D13).

The body is UTF-8 with a BOM and RFC-4180 quoting. Rows are ordered OLDEST-FIRST,
unlike ``GET /transactions``; ``amount``/``base_amount``/``counter_amount`` are
major-unit decimal strings, each at ITS OWN currency's exponent, and the base
pair is the row's STORED snapshot — empty (never zero) when it has none.
Transfers are included (OQ-3), with both account names and the arriving amount.
